text.p: Political uncertainties continued to overshadow the Turkish markets although deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller said that the Islamist-led coalition government would survive, bankers said on Monday.

A persisting cash shortage due to hefty corporate tax payments due end-April also dominated the markets while the central bank intervened for the third day in a row to support the Turkish lira amid political worries over the fate of the government.
Ciller told reporters after meeting Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan that the coalition would continue to work with stability.

Daily Hurriyet quoted former industry and trade minister Yalim Erez, who resigned on Saturday, as saying that the government would collapse in a week's time with the help of other dissidents from the junior coalition partner, the True Path Party (DYP) of Ciller.

Turkish central bank continued to fund banks as the market opened 36.2 trillion lira short. It lent 18.3 trillion lira at 72 percent via overnight, 44.9 trillion lira at 67 percent via tmrw/next and 3.4 trillion lira at 68 percent via tmrw/week deals.
The average overnight money rate firmed to 71.89 percent from Friday's 71.85.
The average overnight repo rate was also high at 74.59 percent which raised the cost of funding for players active in the bond market, bankers said.
"The negative political situation and the high funding cost caused by liquidity shortage are effective. Players prefer to keep cash rather than buy paper," said one banker.

Trade volume was low in the bond market but the yields fell by as much as two percentage points. The most heavily traded papers were April 22 and 29, 1998 which yielded 97.25 percent and 96.98 percent, versus Friday's close of 99.13 and 98.71 percent, respectively.
The central bank continued its string of interventions in the foreign exchange market by buying lira for dollars in the afternoon.

The lira which sank to a low of 135,310 per dollar amid a firmer dollar/mark parity and minor demand, firmed to close at 135,200 after the intervention, but it was weaker on Friday's close of 134,000.
Bankers said the central bank aimed to eliminate the growing gap between the central bank's key dollar rate for banks' compulsory transfers and banks' dollar bids.
Its key dollar rate closed at 134,950 lira, up from 134,900 at midday and the gap dropped to 0.2 percent from previous 0.3.
The central bank had also intervened on Thursday and Friday when dollar demand picked on political concerns following a 6-1/2 day holiday.
On Saturday, two DYP ministers resigned and the National Security Council repeated its demand for the implementation of anti-Islamist measures recommended at its February 28 meeting.

The secularist army was reported to be displeased at Erbakan's reluctance to carry out the measures which had also sparked a row between the Islamist and conservative wings of the 10-month old alliance.
